papers.version_note: arXiv:2312.14904v5, dated 24 Sep 2025 (26 September 2025 on the title page). This is the Review Article submitted to Rep. Prog. Phys., not the 2023 version v1 the file name suggests; the record id carries 2025.
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum algorithms for scientific computing, using electronic structure calculations and computational fluid dynamics as examples, and covering HPC integration issues such as clock speed mismatch and data encoding.

existing.value: The authors state that potential challenges include encoding and decoding classical data for quantum devices and mismatched clock speeds between classical and quantum processors.
quotes: Potential challenges include encoding and decoding classical data for quantum devices, and mismatched clock speeds between classical and quantum processors.

existing.note: Right as stored. The paper gives no citation at this sentence; Table 4 (Section 5.1) lists two-qubit gate speeds from 10 MHz to 10 Hz, which is the same six orders of magnitude, but the sentence itself is the authors' own statement.
existing.value: The authors state that clock speed mismatches between classical and quantum hardware can be up to six orders of magnitude depending on the hardware, and that good programming models for asynchronous computing on these timescales do not yet exist.
quotes: This is compounded by clock speed mismatches that, depending on the type of quantum hardware, can be up to six orders of magnitude.
we do not yet have good programming models for how to handle asynchronous computing on these timescales

existing.note: Right as stored. The 2030 forecast is attributed to companies with no citation given in the sentence.
existing.value: The authors state that standalone quantum hardware will support only niche applications and that interfacing with classical HPC is essential. They also report that companies forecast fully error corrected processors of hundreds or thousands of qubits by 2030.
quotes: However, standalone quantum hardware will support only niche applications.
Companies are forecasting fully error corrected quantum processors on the scale of hundreds or thousands of qubits by 2030

verification and testing [50; 51] (we only cover benchmarks in section 2.7)

quotes: The consensus is that quantum devices will not simply replace HPC.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing hardware is not yet mature enough to integrate seamlessly with HPC.
quotes: Quantum computing hardware is not yet mature enough to seamlessly integrate with HPC

assertions.value: The authors state that current systems are small and imperfect (NISQ) and are not yet powerful enough to solve useful problems, but allow researchers to test and develop quantum algorithms.
quotes: Current systems are small and imperfect, known as noisy, intermediate scale quantum computers (NISQ) [26; 27].
They are not yet powerful enough to solve useful problems, but do allow researchers to test and develop quantum algorithms

assertions.value: The authors state that the supremacy tasks (random circuit sampling and Gaussian boson sampling) are not yet known to have industrial or other useful applications, and that the classical algorithms have since been improved.
quotes: These supremacy tasks are not yet known to have any industrial or other useful applications, and the classical algorithms have since been improved

assertions.value: The authors report, from microprocessor trend data cited from another source, that the growth predicted by Moore's law held until about 2005, when CPU clock speeds reached around 4 GHz.
quotes: The growth predicted was borne out by major chip and computer system vendors until about 2005, when CPU clock speeds reached around 4 GHz (Figure 1).

assertions.value: The authors state that, as of June 2024, Frontier and Aurora are the only true exascale machines worldwide.
quotes: As of June 2024, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Frontier system and Argonne National Laboratory’s Aurora system are the only true exascale machines worldwide.

assertions.value: The authors state that novel hardware systems, including quantum computing, will be required to extend global computational capacity significantly beyond current capabilities.
quotes: Novel hardware systems, including quantum computing, will be required to significantly extend global computational capacity beyond current capabilities.

assertions.value: The authors state that the no-cloning theorem says it is impossible to make copies of unknown quantum states.
quotes: the no-cloning theorem [61] states that it is impossible to make copies of unknown quantum states.

assertions.value: The authors state that the subset of gates that are efficiently classically simulable, and so not sufficient for universal quantum computing, are known as Clifford gates, and that adding a T gate or a Z-rotation with a well-chosen angle is sufficient for universal quantum computing.
quotes: The subset of gates that are efficiently classically simulable and thus not sufficient for universal quantum computing are known as Clifford gates
The addition of a T gate or a Z-rotation with a well-chosen angle is sufficient to generate universal quantum computing.

assertions.value: The authors state that many physical qubits are needed for quantum error correction to produce one logical qubit.
quotes: Many physical qubits are needed for quantum error correction procedures [49] to produce one logical qubit to perform useful computations.

assertions.value: The authors report that Reiher et al. estimated 313 physical qubits per logical qubit for the FeMoco simulation if there is one error for every 109 quantum gates (exponent printed flat), and that the authors expect thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, or much better error rates, for complicated real-world simulations.
quotes: They estimated 313 physical qubits are needed for each logical qubit, if there is one error for every 109 quantum gates.
we would likely need thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, or much better error rates, for complicated real-world quantum chemistry simulations
assertions.reader_inference: The second quote is the authors' extrapolation, not Reiher et al.'s result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the DiVincenzo requirements for scalable quantum computing remain relevant: scalable well-characterized qubits, qubit initialization, long decoherence times, a universal gate set, and qubit measurement.
quotes: The requirements for scalable quantum computing laid out by DiVincenzo [63] are still relevant today: scalable, well-characterized qubits;

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum Fourier transform has an exponential speed-up with complexity of order the square of log N, against order N log N for the fast Fourier transform, for problem size N.
quotes: It is the quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform and has exponential speed-up (complexity O((log N )2)) compared to the fast Fourier transform’s O(N log N ) complexity

assertions.value: The authors state that the QFT stores its result as amplitudes, so measurements identify individual Fourier components and the QFT is not directly useful for determining the Fourier-transformed coefficients of the original list.
quotes: The QFT performs a discrete Fourier transform on a list of complex numbers encoded as the amplitudes of a quantum state vector.
Measurements performed on the quantum state identify individual Fourier components

assertions.value: The authors state that the QFT requires a number of elementary gates of order n squared (printed O(n2)) for n qubits.
quotes: Hence the QFT requires O(n2) elementary gates in total.

assertions.value: The authors state that the semi-classical nature of the QFT circuit means it can be efficiently simulated on classical computers when used at the start or end of a quantum computation.
quotes: The semi-classical nature of the QFT circuit means it can be efficiently simulated on classical computers [68; 69] when used at either the start or end of a quantum computation.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum phase estimation is equivalent to simulating quantum system dynamics.
quotes: Quantum phase estimation is equivalent to simulating quantum system dynamics.

assertions.value: The authors state that the standard QPE circuit is unsuitable for early fault-tolerant quantum computers, which can implement only low circuit depths and limited numbers of logical qubits.
quotes: The QPE algorithm in Figure 6 is unsuitable for early fault-tolerant quantum computers since these devices can only implement low circuit depths and limited numbers of logical qubits [72].

assertions.value: The authors state that Shor's algorithm showed factoring could be solved by quantum computers in polynomial time, and so lets a large enough future quantum computer break RSA encryption.
quotes: Shor’s algorithm showed that factoring could be solved by quantum computers in polynomial time.
It provided a way for large enough (future) quantum computers to break RSA encryption [75]

assertions.value: The authors state that classical computers have factored semiprimes up to 829 bits long, and that quantum computers large enough to beat this are still some way into the future because of error correction overheads.
quotes: Classical computers have to date factored semiprimes up to 829 bits long [76].
However, quantum computers large enough to beat this are still some way into the future.

assertions.value: The authors state that Grover's algorithm generally provides a square root speed up over classical search.
quotes: Grover’s algorithm generally provides a square root speed up over a classical search

assertions.value: The authors state that Grover's algorithm is only of practical use where the oracle function can be evaluated efficiently, which can happen when it is a subroutine but is not generally possible when the data are classical.
quotes: Consequently, Grover’s algorithm is only of practical use in situations where we can perform the oracle function efficiently
but is not generally possible when the data are classical.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first proven speed ups for quantum walk algorithms were a quadratic speed up for a search algorithm and an exponential speed up, with respect to an oracle, for transport across a particular type of disordered graph.
quotes: with a search algorithm [79] equivalent to Grover’s algorithm [14] providing a quadratic speed up, and an algorithm for transport across a particular type of disordered graph [93] that provides an exponential speed up with respect to an oracle.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum walks provide models of universal quantum computing but are not suitable for physical implementation, and are mostly useful for complexity proofs.
quotes: Quantum walks also provide models of universal quantum computing [97; 98], but they are not suitable for physical implementation.

assertions.value: The authors state that HHL requires efficient preparation of the state |b> by loading the vector components, which is in general not trivial, and that it is not possible to efficiently recover the full solution |x>, only expectation values of an operator.
quotes: Key examples include the requirement to be able to efficiently prepare the state |b⟩ by somehow loading the vector components into the quantum computer.
However, even if these requirements are met, it is not possible to efficiently recover the full solution |x⟩.

assertions.value: The authors state that extracting the individual components of |x> is costly and can severely mitigate the speedup offered by HHL, so that direct application to classical problems needs detailed consideration of the data-transfer bottlenecks.
quotes: Moreover, extracting the individual components of |x⟩ is a costly process that can severely mitigate the inherent speedup offered by the HHL algorithm [58].
direct application to classical problems requires detailed consideration of the bottlenecks associated with data transfer between classical and quantum realms [125]

assertions.value: The authors state that QPE remains a bottleneck in HHL, requiring order 1/epsilon applications of a unitary to reach precision epsilon, so that even with the fastest Hamiltonian simulation the overall improvement would likely be modest.
quotes: QPE remains a bottleneck by requiring O(1/ϵ) applications of a unitary operation to estimate its eigenvalues to precision ϵ.
the overall improvement would likely be modest

assertions.value: The authors state that decomposing the inverse operator into a linear combination of unitaries using Fourier or Chebyshev expansions exponentially improves the dependence on the precision parameter.
quotes: This approach exponentially improves dependence on the precision parameter

assertions.value: The authors state that for the iterative-HHL approach the convergence rate for more general cases remains uncertain.
quotes: However, the convergence rate for more general cases remains uncertain.

assertions.value: The authors state that HHL is an important subroutine in many quantum machine learning algorithms, including quantum support vector machines, quantum principal component analysis and quantum recommendation systems.
quotes: There are many quantum machine learning algorithms where HHL is an important subroutine, such as data classification using quantum support vector machines [115]

assertions.value: The authors state that many optimization problems can be expressed as QUBO problems, and that classical optimization problems can be mapped to finding the ground state of a classical Ising Hamiltonian.
quotes: Many optimization problems can be expressed as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems.
Conveniently, classical optimization problems can be efficiently mapped to finding the ground state of a classical Ising Hamiltonian [132; 133].

assertions.value: The authors state that adiabatic quantum computing is inherently robust against noise and, with more general Hamiltonians, computationally equivalent to gate-based quantum computers.
quotes: A useful property of AQC is that it is inherently robust against noise [135].
it is computationally equivalent to gate-based quantum computers [136]

assertions.value: The authors state that the adiabatic conditions imposed by AQC are rarely met in reality, since meeting them would need long, inefficient and impractical run times.
quotes: in reality, the adiabatic conditions imposed by AQC are rarely met.
Meeting them would require long run times that are inefficient and impractical.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational algorithms are beneficial for NISQ devices: many repeats of a shallow circuit avoid the need for long coherence times, and parameter tuning can compensate for several types of errors.
quotes: It is possible to use many separate repeats of a shallow (short) quantum circuit.
This avoids the need for long coherence times.

assertions.value: The authors state that many proposed QAOA techniques rely on heuristics and empirical observations rather than theoretical guarantees, and that most studies are in the few-stage regime where the theoretical results do not apply and so rest on numerical simulations.
quotes: Note that many proposed techniques rely on heuristics and empirical observations rather than theoretical guarantees.
Most studies focus on the few-stage regime where the theoretical results don’t apply and are thus based on numerical simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state that Brady et al. showed QAOA converges to an optimal quantum annealing schedule in the limit of many stages, and that Gerblich et al. showed a sequence of quantum walks also approximates optimal quantum annealing in that limit with better convergence for the same number of stages.
quotes: put the method on a sound theoretical base by showing that QAOA converges to an optimal quantum annealing schedule in the limit of many stages.
also approximates optimal quantum annealing in the limit of many stages, and shows better convergence for the same number of stages.
assertions.reader_inference: Gerblich et al. [163] includes author V. Kendon of this review.

assertions.value: The authors state that each round of classical optimization needs at least one quantum run, so optimization costs must be counted to assess the full quantum cost, and that ignoring them can distort the apparent scaling in numerical results.
quotes: It is important to count the optimization costs correctly to assess the full quantum cost, since each round of classical optimization requires at least one quantum run to evaluate the cost function.
show how ignoring optimization costs can distort the apparent scaling in numerical results

assertions.value: The authors state that, by the Rayleigh-Ritz principle, the lowest eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator is upper-bounded by the minimum expectation value found by varying the state, which is the basis of VQE.
quotes: The Rayleigh-Ritz principle states that the lowest eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator Hˆ is upper-bounded

assertions.value: The authors state that direct simulation by a unitary circuit increases circuit depth polynomially with evolution time, which is difficult in hardware with short coherence times, and that variational simulation aims to obtain a shorter circuit.
quotes: However, this increases the circuit depth polynomially with respect to the evolution time t [168] which is difficult to achieve in hardware with short coherence times.
The aim is to obtain a shorter circuit than would be needed for direct simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum neural networks can offload nonlinearities to classical computers or use quantum kernels, and are similar to kernel methods.
quotes: QNNs can offload nonlinearities to classical computers, or use quantum kernels.
There are similarities between QNNs and kernel methods [178; 174], which are well-established machine learning techniques.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main advantage of variational circuits arises from the feature map, and that when the feature map cannot be simulated efficiently on classical computers the overall quantum speedup can be up to exponential.
quotes: The main advantage of variational circuits actually arises from the feature map:
the overall quantum speedup can be up to exponential.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence gives no condition on the data or the model, and no proof or measurement; it reads as a conditional upper bound on possible speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational quantum algorithms face a trade-off between expressivity and trainability, that performance decreases significantly as qubit number and circuit depth increase, and that large depth gives the optimizer noisy gradient information that can lead to divergence or barren plateaus.
quotes: In general, there is a trade-off between the expressivity and trainability of the circuit [188].
Performance decreases significantly when qubit number and circuit depth increase.

assertions.value: The authors state that the barren plateau phenomenon occurs when the non-convex loss landscape becomes exponentially flat on average as qubit number increases, and that the effects on parameter optimization can potentially destroy any quantum speedup.
quotes: The barren plateau phenomenon occurs when the non-convex loss function landscape becomes exponentially flat (on average) as qubit number increases.
The effects on parameter optimization can potentially destroy any quantum speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that hand optimization tends to beat the generic automated compilers for specific applications, and that gate-by-gate programming is about equivalent to assembler code for classical computers.
quotes: Indeed, hand optimization will tend to beat the automated compilers for specific applications (the automated compilers are generic)
Programming gate by gate is very low level, about equivalent to assembler code for classical computers

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum software start-ups promise seamless integration into existing programming languages, that HPC users know this is hype, and that good performance needs consideration of how to map an application to the hardware.
quotes: HPC users will be well aware that this is hype.
Good performance is only achieved with some consideration of how best to map an application to the hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that higher level tools to map a problem to the hardware graph across 5,000 qubits are available but do not necessarily beat a hand-crafted assignment for specific problems.
quotes: Higher level tools to map the problem to the hardware graph across 5,000 qubits are available [227; 228], but do not necessarily beat a hand-crafted assignment for specific problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that low-level benchmarks alone can label a slow high-fidelity quantum computer as equivalent to a fast low-fidelity one, and that extrapolating from low-level to higher-level performance is unreliable.
quotes: Using low-level benchmarks alone can label a slow high-fidelity quantum computer as equivalent to a fast low-fidelity quantum computer [245].
extrapolating from low level performance to higher level is unreliable.

assertions.value: The authors state that FLOPS and CLOPS should not be converted between, because they do not correspond to the same unit of computation.
quotes: It does not make sense to convert between the two metrics, since they do not correspond to the same unit of computation.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical simulation of ideal quantum circuits in full generality is limited to about 45 qubits because Hilbert space grows exponentially with qubit number.
quotes: albeit limited to about 45 qubits in full generality due to the exponential size of Hilbert space in qubit number.

assertions.value: The authors state that subsequent classical work brought the classical runtime for Google's random circuit task down by some orders of magnitude, that similar advances occurred for boson sampling, and that comparing against the best classical algorithm is not enough to establish quantum advantage.
quotes: Subsequent work brought down the classical runtime by some orders of magnitude [285; 286; 287].
Similar advances have occurred with boson sampling [296; 297; 298].
Comparing state-of-the-art quantum computers with the best classical algorithm for the same problem is not enough to establish a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that if a dequantized classical algorithm exists for a quantum machine learning algorithm, the quantum counterpart cannot give an exponential speedup on classical data.
quotes: If a dequantized algorithm exists, then its quantum counterpart cannot give an exponential speedup on classical data.

assertions.value: The authors state that many QML algorithms make different assumptions from the classical algorithms they are compared with, and that claimed quantum speed-ups often neglect the encoding step in the runtime while comparing against classical algorithms on raw unprocessed data.
quotes: Many quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms make different assumptions from the classical algorithms they are compared with [58].
Breakthroughs that claim a quantum speed-up often neglect the quantum encoding step in the algorithm runtime

assertions.value: The authors state that dequantization shows classical sampling techniques can potentially yield a classical algorithm that runs exponentially faster than any other known classical algorithm.
quotes: dequantization shows how replacing quantum linear algebra algorithms with classical sampling techniques can potentially create a classical algorithm that runs exponentially faster than any other known classical algorithm [295].

assertions.value: The authors state that current research predicts a narrow window in qubit number where circuit-model NISQ hardware can potentially outperform classical hardware for certain problems, since errors build up without active error correction.
quotes: Current research predicts a narrow window in terms of the number of qubits where circuit model NISQ hardware can potentially outperform classical hardware for certain problems [299].
Errors inevitably build up and render the computation unreliable without active error correction.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent proof-of-concept studies of quantum error correction begin to show errors suppressed for extended gate sequences.
quotes: Recent proof-of-concept studies of quantum error correction [300; 301] begin to show errors suppressed for extended gate sequences

assertions.value: The authors state that Trotterization needs small time steps for acceptable precision, which requires many gates and extremely deep circuits, well beyond NISQ capabilities for useful problem sizes.
quotes: Acceptable precision comes at the expense of small ∆t, which requires many quantum gates and hence extremely deep circuits, well beyond NISQ capabilities for useful problem sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state, in the comparison table of analogue and digital simulation, that digital quantum simulation requires high depth circuits and is unlikely to be practical before fully error corrected quantum computers are available.
quotes: Requires high depth circuits (many quantum gates) therefore unlikely to be practical before fully error corrected quantum computers are available.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Monte Carlo often needs millions of samples, taking hours or days on current HPC, and that in fermionic systems it can suffer from the sign problem, a lack of convergence in the sampling.
quotes: often on the order of millions of samples, which can take hours or even days on current HPC.
where enforcing fermion exchange statistics leads to a lack of convergence in the QMC sampling

assertions.value: The authors state that many lattice gauge theory simulations on NISQ hardware require removing redundant degrees of freedom or imposing symmetries, and that such simplifications are essential in the resource-limited NISQ era.
quotes: many lattice gauge theory simulations on NISQ hardware require fully or partially removing redundant degrees of freedom or imposing symmetries.

assertions.value: The authors state that the possibility of an exponential quantum advantage for quantum chemistry remains controversial in practice, and that it is challenging to beat the best classical computations given decades of work on classical methods.
quotes: In practice, the possibility of achieving an exponential quantum advantage for quantum chemistry problems remains controversial [340].
given the decades of work already done on classical methods for quantum systems.

assertions.value: The authors state that fault-tolerant quantum computers are predicted to solve the electronic structure problem in polynomial time, and that a quantum advantage may exist even without a clear polynomial scaling.
quotes: Fault-tolerant quantum computers are predicted to solve the electronic structure problem for many-body systems [338] in polynomial time
It is possible that a quantum advantage exists even in the absence of a clear polynomial scaling.

quotes: Modern computational chemistry aims to simulate molecules and materials within 1 kcal/mol accuracy
such a level of precision can only be achieved for small systems

assertions.value: The authors state that calculating partition functions of physical systems is generally #P-hard, so both classical and quantum methods are unlikely to provide exact solutions.
quotes: Calculating partition functions of physical systems is generally a #P-hard complexity class problem [343; 344]

quotes: to calculate the atomization energy of the strongly correlated square H4 molecule.
The results are competitive with those of the state-of-the-art classical methods.
which is a non-trivial step.

quotes: DFT is system-specific and does not reach the desired chemical accuracy.
this method has the disadvantage of self-interaction

assertions.value: The authors state that NISQ devices limit the basis set size because of hardware constraints, so basis set size becomes a more significant limit on accuracy than on classical computers.
quotes: In contrast, NISQ devices impose limitations on the basis set size due to hardware constraints [359]

assertions.value: The authors state that full configuration interaction scales combinatorially and can only be performed on classical computers for small systems.
quotes: It can only be performed on classical computers for small systems.

while QPE assumes the ansatz has a reasonable overlap with the exact ground state

quotes: ADAPT-VQE produces hardware-friendly circuits with few entangling gates, but the present technological limitations make it necessary to consider variants of ADAPT-VQE to enhance its performance.

quotes: On NISQ devices, FCI is suitable for small molecules such as H2 and LiH [339]

results in a significant reduction in the gate count, but requires a large number of measurements, which are only possible for small systems.

quotes: who estimate the resources to simulate the time dynamics on a 5 × 5 square lattice to ≤ 10% accuracy require 50 qubits and 1,243,586 standard two-qubit gates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the FeMoco active space contains 54 electrons in 108 spin orbitals, and that proposed computational models of FeMoco are beyond current classical methods but possible with small error-corrected quantum computers.
quotes: The FeMoco active space contains 54 electrons in 108 spin orbitals.
Proposed computational models of FeMoco are beyond the reach of current classical methods but are possible with small error-corrected quantum computers.

tum computer equipped with 4 × 106 physical qubits

a condition which is not true for real fluids.

assertions.value: The authors state that a primary obstacle to quantum LB algorithms is the need to measure during the simulation, and that Todorova and Steijl forgo the complete flow field and obtain only specific information such as particle number densities, with measurement postponed to the end.
quotes: A primary obstacle to quantum LB algorithms is the need to take measurements during the simulation.
algorithm does not obtain a complete picture of the classical state.

assertions.value: The authors state that a revised quantum lattice gas algorithm removes repeated measurements at each time step, but its required quantum register scales linearly with the number of lattice sites, which makes realistic use cases hard to reach.
quotes: However, the size of the required quantum register scales linearly with the number of lattice sites.
This makes it difficult to scale to realistic use cases.

assertions.value: The authors state that a fully unitary streaming and collision operator has a sub-optimal dependence on the number of time steps, that Budinski's algorithm is restricted to a single time step before reinitialization because of nonlinearity, and that conventional amplitude and basis encodings do not allow unitary operators for both streaming and collision.
quotes: However, their collision step has a sub-optimal dependence on the number of time steps.
the resulting nonlinearity restricts the algorithm to a single time-step before the state must be reinitialized.
the conventional amplitude and basis encodings do not allow unitary operators for both streaming and collision.

assertions.value: The authors state that the SPH method is considered computationally expensive, and that one strategy to address its bottlenecks is to use quantum subroutines such as quantum inner-product estimation and Grover-type neighbour search.
quotes: One strategy to address these bottlenecks involves using quantum subroutines [514].
This is another major bottleneck that we can, in principle, address using Grover’s search algorithm [14] implemented with a quantum walk

assertions.value: The authors state that SPH time steps are of order 10−5 seconds or less, typically about one million steps per simulated second, and that a quantum algorithm able to evolve many time steps between measurements has the best chance of providing real advantages.
quotes: This leads to timesteps of the order of ≤ 10−5 seconds [512], or typically one million time steps to simulate one second of physical time.
A quantum algorithm that can evolve for many time steps between measurements has the best chance of providing real advantages.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the classical part of a hybrid scheme needs consistent feedback from the quantum part, the cost of measurement and reloading input states may significantly reduce any quantum advantage.
quotes: However, if the classical part then requires consistent feedback from the quantum part, the cost of measurement and reloading input states may significantly reduce any quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report that a hybrid quantum physics-informed neural network with a quantum depth infused layer and transfer learning reported a 21% reduction in loss compared with its classical counterpart.
quotes: a hybrid quantum PINN based on a quantum depth infused layer implemented using a VQA and coupled with transfer learning.
The authors reported a 21% reduction in loss compared with its purely classical counterpart.

assertions.value: The authors state that many existing demonstrations of quantum CFD algorithms are limited to relatively simple flow cases, and that scaling with the Reynolds number is either yet to be established or appears limited.
quotes: many existing demonstrations of quantum algorithms for CFD are limited to relatively simple flow cases.
The effectiveness of these algorithms at scaling with the Reynolds number is either yet to be established or appears limited.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum-inspired algorithm using Schmidt decomposition and tensor network methods can successfully account for interscale correlations in turbulence, which benefits classical simulation even if useful quantum turbulence simulation is far off.
quotes: a quantum-inspired algorithm using Schmidt decomposition combined with tensor network methods can successfully account for the interscale correlations in turbulence [545].

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum clock speed cannot be defined as the inverse of the gate layer time, because gate choice varies durations and quantum error correction overheads, dominated by mid-circuit measurements, are likely to dominate the runtime of large machines.
quotes: However we cannot define the quantum clock speed as an inverse of the quantum gate layer time because of two major variables:
Large-scale quantum computers will likely have a runtime dominated by quantum error correction (QEC) overheads.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate (Table 4) conservative estimates of two-qubit gate speed and measurement time for six hardware platforms, ordered by decreasing gate speed, from 10 MHz to 10 Hz for gates; they state these are physical gate speeds that error correction overheads will significantly modify.
quotes: Table 4: Quantum hardware platforms ordered by decreasing gate speed (conservative estimates).
two-qubit gate speed 10 MHz
6 MHz 750 kHz 6 kHz 170 Hz 10 Hz
Note that these are physical gate speeds that error correction overheads will significantly modify.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical CPU clock speeds have stayed around 3 GHz for the last decade, significantly faster than any current quantum hardware, and that quantum hardware cannot follow Moore's law-style clock increases because atoms, ions and electrons have intrinsic frequencies that cannot be made smaller.
quotes: Classical CPU clock speeds have remained around 3 GHz over the last decade, which is significantly faster than any current quantum hardware.
Individual atoms, ions or electrons have their own intrinsic physical frequencies which cannot be made smaller.

assertions.value: The authors state that a hybrid algorithm may need to queue 100 or 104 (exponent printed flat) operations on the classical processor for every operation on the quantum processor, which they consider viable for some large multi-scale simulations.
quotes: A hybrid algorithm may need to queue 100 or 104 operations on the classical processor for every operation on the quantum processor.
This should be viable for some of the large, multi-scale simulations that dominate today’s HPC use

assertions.value: The authors report that Madsen et al. performed boson sampling in 36 µs via a 216-mode squeezed photon state, and state that this platform cannot perform universal quantum computing.
quotes: Madsen et al. [549] performed boson sampling in just 36 µs via a 216-mode squeezed photon state.
although it cannot perform universal quantum computing.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude encoding stores exponentially many real values in n qubits, but manipulating individual amplitudes needs exponentially many gates, arbitrary state preparation is expensive, and approximate amplitude encoding reduces the cost to polynomial in n at the cost of accuracy.
quotes: However, to manipulate individual amplitudes, the number of gates grows exponentially with qubit number.
Preparing an arbitrary state is thus an expensive operation [558; 559; 560].
reduces the preparation cost to O(poly(n)) gates for n qubits at a cost of reduced accuracy

assertions.value: The authors state that angle encoding is easy to prepare but the angle values cannot be read out from a single measurement on a single copy of the qubit.
quotes: However, it is not possible to read out the value of the angles using a single measurement on a single copy of the qubit.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRAM performs a memory access over all addresses in order log N time at the cost of order N ancillary qubits, but it is still uncertain whether QRAM can achieve quantum speedups in principle or in practice, and that it is sensitive to decoherence and error-correction overhead.
quotes: QRAM performs the operation in (59) in O(log N ) time at the cost of O(N ) ancillary qubits.
However, it is still uncertain whether QRAM can be used to achieve quantum speedups, in principle or in practice [58; 569].
QRAM is sensitive to decoherence [570] and is subject to an overhead associated with error correction of ancillary qubits [571].

assertions.value: The authors state that Hamiltonian encoding is straightforward to implement but the required precision increases with problem size, and not every problem maps easily onto Ising parameters.
quotes: Although straightforward to implement, the required precision increases with the problem size.
not every problem can be easily mapped on to the Ising Hamiltonian parameters.

assertions.value: The authors state that domain-wall encoding is efficient in NISQ devices for variables with a small fixed range of values.
quotes: Domain wall encoding is efficient in NISQ devices for variables with a small fixed range of values [582].

assertions.value: The authors state that transferring data and instructions from room temperature into cryogenic hardware is a significant issue because signals carry heat in, which constrains code to minimize data exchange, and that re-cooling and calibration make the quantum processors unavailable.
quotes: A significant issue is transferring data and instructions from room temperature to the cryogenic conditions required for operating many types of quantum hardware.
minimizing data exchange to reduce cooling costs

assertions.value: The authors state that qubit readout timescales are even slower than the quantum clock speeds, and these factors significantly affect the wallclock time of algorithms.
quotes: Slower quantum “clock speeds” (section 5.1) are accompanied by even slower timescales for measurements to read out the qubit state

assertions.value: The authors state that the most important next step for integrating quantum computers with HPC is making test bed hardware widely available.
quotes: The most important next step for integrating quantum computers with HPC is making test bed hardware widely available [546; 547].

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum equivalent of Moore's law can already be identified in steady improvements in qubit number and quality, most evident in superconducting qubits and ion traps.
quotes: it is already possible to identify a quantum equivalent of Moore’s Law through the steady improvements in the qubit number and quality (Figure 21).

assertions.value: The authors state that IBM announced a chip with over a thousand physical qubits, that further progress needs error correction, and that each such chip will contain only a few logical qubits.
quotes: IBM recently announced their newest quantum chip, which provides over a thousand physical qubits [586]
each of IBM’s thousand-qubit chips will contain only a few of these logical qubits
assertions.reader_inference: This is the paper's own statement about logical qubits per chip, and it sits next to the forecast of hundreds or thousands of error corrected qubits by 2030.

assertions.value: The authors state that IonQ's latest systems have up to 32 qubits, with 64 qubit systems due in 2025.
quotes: IonQ’s latest systems have up to 32 qubits, with 64 qubit systems due in 2025.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is by no means clear that superconducting qubits or ion traps will be the main hardware type in the longer term, and that an ecosystem of several hardware types for different applications is plausible.
quotes: it is by no means clear they will turn out to be the main type of quantum hardware in the longer term.
An ecosystem that supports several types of hardware for different applications is both plausible and promising.

assertions.value: The authors state that, despite significant engineering challenges, there is growing confidence that the hardware will deliver on the anticipated timescales.
quotes: there is growing confidence that the hardware will deliver on the anticipated timescales.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most important interfacing challenges are the data encodings natural for quantum computers, that data conversion and transfer are largely an engineering challenge, and that commercial promises of seamless software integration are plausible for test beds but have no assured path to scale.
quotes: The most important are related to the different data encodings that are natural for quantum computers
While data conversion and transfer are largely an engineering challenge
but do not yet have an assured path for scaling up.

assertions.value: The authors state that redesigning codes for GPUs was extremely challenging and time-consuming, that quantum processors will be significantly more challenging to deploy alongside classical HPC at scale, and that the investment needed is a significant barrier to adoption.
quotes: Quantum processors will be significantly more challenging still to deploy alongside classical HPC at scale.
The investment of time and resources necessary to leverage quantum computing is a significant barrier to widespread adoption

assertions.value: The authors state that for HHL, quantum lattice Boltzmann and SPH, the proposed quantum approaches avoid reading out the complete field, for example by computing in situ nonlinear functions such as the average viscous dissipation rate.
quotes: Instead of simply measuring out the complete velocity field, the authors propose a novel quantum postprocessing protocol for efficiently computing in situ nonlinear functions of the resulting flow field, namely the average viscous dissipation rate.
